title: Retraction of a faithfully flat ind-étale algebra over a w-contractible ring
statement:
Let $R$ be w-contractible [det-pe-wlocal-strict-contractible] and $R\to B$ faithfully flat
and ind-étale. Let $B'$ be as in [det-pe-wc-rings-w-local-refinement] and
$T=(\operatorname{Spec}B')^c$. Then there is a closed subset $T'\subset T$ mapping
homeomorphically onto $(\operatorname{Spec}R)^c$, and for any such $T'$ the composite
$R\to B'\to B'':=B'_{[T']}$ is an isomorphism. In particular
$B\to B'\to B''\cong R$ is an $R$-algebra retraction of $R\to B$.

proof.text: Write $X^c=(\operatorname{Spec}R)^c$ and $T=(\operatorname{Spec}B')^c$. By [det-pe-wlocal-strict-contractible], $R$ is w-local and $X^c$ is extremally disconnected. The refinement [det-pe-wc-rings-w-local-refinement] makes $\operatorname{Spec}B'$ w-local and sends all its closed points to closed points of $\operatorname{Spec}R$, surjectively. The continuous spectrum map therefore restricts to a continuous surjection $p:T\to X^c$. By [det-pe-wlocal-components], both closed-point spaces are profinite, hence compact Hausdorff. Apply clause (3) of [det-pe-stonean-projective] to obtain a continuous $\sigma:X^c\to T$ with $p\sigma=\mathrm{id}$.

source.place: Choice of components, first four sentences

proof.text: Set $T'=\sigma(X^c)$. Its points are exactly the fixed points of $\sigma p:T\to T$: one implication uses $p\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ and the other writes a fixed point as $\sigma(p(t))$. This set is closed: for a nonfixed $t$, choose disjoint neighborhoods of $t$ and $\sigma p(t)$ in the Hausdorff space $T$; intersect the first with the inverse image of the second under $\sigma p$ to obtain an open neighborhood disjoint from the fixed-point set. Since $T$ is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}B'$ by w-locality, $T'$ is also Zariski closed there. The restrictions of $p$ and $\sigma$ are continuous inverse maps between $T'$ and $X^c$, proving the required homeomorphism.

source.place: Choice of components, last sentence, with closedness and inverse written explicitly

proof.text: Now fix ANY closed subset $T'\subseteq T$ for which $p|_{T'}$ is a homeomorphism onto $X^c$, not just the image chosen above. It is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}B'$ because $T$ is closed. Put $C=B''=B'_{[T']}$, with its canonical $R$-algebra map $f:R\to C$. By [lem-weil-pbc-retained-localization], $B'\to C$ is ind-Zariski, $C$ is w-local, its closed points are indexed by $t\in T'$, its primes are pairs $(t,y)$ with $y\subseteq t$, and $C_{(t,y)}\cong B'_y$ canonically. An ind-Zariski map is ind-étale by its presentation in [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. Since $R\to B'$ is ind-étale by [det-pe-wc-rings-w-local-refinement], composition stability in [lem-weil-pbc-ind-etale-stability] makes $f$ ind-étale, hence weakly étale. The definition of weakly étale in [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra] in particular makes $f$ flat.

source.place: The algebra B double prime, both sentences

proof.text: For $t\in T'$ write $\widetilde t$ for its corresponding closed point of $\operatorname{Spec}C$ and $\mathfrak m=p(t)$. The contraction of $\widetilde t$ to $R$ is $\mathfrak m$, because the retained point is $(t,t)$ and its contraction to $B'$ is $t$. The ring $R_{\mathfrak m}$ is strictly henselian by [det-pe-wlocal-strict-contractible]. Apply [det-pe-wc-rings-local-iso] to the weakly étale map $R\to C$, the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and the prime $\widetilde t$ above it: the CANONICAL map $R_{\mathfrak m}\to C_{\widetilde t}$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Bijectivity on spectra and local rings, first two sentences

proof.text:
By [lem-weil-pbc-primes-of-localization], primes of $C_{\widetilde t}$ correspond, by contraction, to primes of $C$ contained in $\widetilde t$, and primes of $R_{\mathfrak m}$ to primes of $R$ contained in $\mathfrak m$. The canonical isomorphism of the preceding step therefore gives a bijection between these two sets of generalizations. Every prime of either w-local ring lies under exactly one maximal ideal, by [det-pe-wlocal-strict-contractible]; the maximal ideals of $C$ are indexed by $T'$, and $T'	o X^c$ is bijective. Taking the union of the preceding bijections over these disjoint sets gives bijectivity of $\operatorname{Spec}C	o\operatorname{Spec}R$. Moreover if $\mathfrak q\subseteq\widetilde t$ contracts to $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak m$, localize $R_{\mathfrak m}\cong C_{\widetilde t}$ at the corresponding primes. The resulting localizations are $R_{\mathfrak p}$ and $C_{\mathfrak q}$. Indeed, for $A=R$ or $C$, with the corresponding primes $P\subseteq M$, a fraction $a/s\in A_M$ belongs to $PA_M$ exactly when $a\in P$, since $s
otin M$ and $P\subseteq M$. In the iterated localization the mutually inverse fraction maps are $(a/s)/(b/t)\mapsto at/(sb)$ and $a/u\mapsto(a/1)/(u/1)$; here $b,u
otin P$ and $s,t
otin M$, so all displayed denominators are allowed. These formulas identify the structural maps, as also supplied by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-of-localization]. Hence the canonical $R_{\mathfrak p}	o C_{\mathfrak q}$ is an isomorphism for every prime $\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Bijectivity on spectra and local rings, remaining sentences

proof.text:
Fix $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$ and its unique inverse image $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}C$. Put $S=f(R\setminus\mathfrak p)$ and $D=S^{-1}C$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-spectrum-embedding], the primes of $D$ correspond to primes $\mathfrak q'$ of $C$ whose contractions $\mathfrak p'$ lie inside $\mathfrak p$: disjointness from $S$ is exactly that containment. Going down for the flat map $f$, supplied by [lem-sc-flat-going-down], gives a prime $\mathfrak q''\subseteq\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak p'$. Injectivity on spectra gives $\mathfrak q''=\mathfrak q'$, so every such $\mathfrak q'$ is contained in $\mathfrak q$. The fractions with numerator in $\mathfrak q$ form a proper prime ideal $Q=\mathfrak qD$: denominators avoid $\mathfrak q$, and $c/s\in Q$ exactly when $c\in\mathfrak q$. For well-definedness, an equality $c/s=c'/s'$ gives $v(s' c-sc')=0$ for some $v\in S$; primality and $v,s,s'
otin\mathfrak q$ show $c\in\mathfrak q$ if and only if $c'\in\mathfrak q$. The same membership test proves $Q$ proper and prime. Every prime of $D$ is contained in $Q$, since every numerator of a fraction in it lies in its contraction $\mathfrak q'\subseteq\mathfrak q$. A maximal ideal containing $Q$ exists by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal]; since it is also contained in $Q$, it equals $Q$. Thus $Q$ is the unique maximal ideal of $D$. For each $c
otin\mathfrak q$, $c/1$ is a unit in $D$: otherwise its proper principal ideal lies in a maximal ideal by the same cited lemma, necessarily $\mathfrak qD$, contradicting contraction to $\mathfrak q$. The map $D	o C_{\mathfrak q}$ sends $c/s$ to $c/s$ because $S\cap\mathfrak q=\varnothing$. Its inverse sends $c/u\in C_{\mathfrak q}$ to $(c/1)(u/1)^{-1}\in D$, using the units just proved for $u
otin\mathfrak q$. The fraction equality relations make both maps well-defined; each composite fixes $c/1$ and every inverted denominator, hence fixes every fraction. They commute with $R_{\mathfrak p}$, so the localized map $R_{\mathfrak p}	o D$ is the isomorphism $R_{\mathfrak p}	o C_{\mathfrak q}$ established above.

source.place: R to B double prime is an isomorphism, localization and going-down argument; expanded fraction inverses

proof.text: Regard $f:R\to C$ as an $R$-linear map. Its module localization at $\mathfrak p$ is exactly $R_{\mathfrak p}\to f(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}C$ from the preceding step: both send $r/s$ to $f(r)/f(s)$, and the module and ring localizations of $C$ have the identical fraction relation $c/s=c'/s'$ if some $u\notin\mathfrak p$ annihilates $f(s')c-f(s)c'$, as in [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. These maps are bijective for all primes, in particular all maximal ideals. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-linear-map-bijective-at-maximal-localizations] to conclude that $f$ is bijective, hence a ring isomorphism. Its inverse is an $R$-algebra isomorphism because $f$ is the structural map.

source.place: R to B double prime is an isomorphism, initial local criterion, completed after the localized calculation

proof.text: Let $j:B\to B'\to C$ be the composite. The map $\rho=f^{-1}j:B\to R$ is an $R$-algebra map. For every $r\in R$, the structural compatibilities give $j(r)=f(r)$, and therefore $\rho(r)=f^{-1}(f(r))=r$. This is the required retraction. The choice in step 3 was arbitrary, so the isomorphism assertion holds for every $T'$ specified in the statement.

source.place: Final displayed composite and retraction identity
